h1: The 6 Best Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Combos of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Wireless Ergonomic Combos: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six wireless ergonomic keyboard and mouse combos, wave, vertical and quiet designs, with picks by budget and desk setup.
mainKeyword: wireless ergonomic keyboard and mouse combos
summary: The Logitech Wave Keys and Lift combo is the best ergonomic set, pairing a wave keyboard with a vertical mouse and connecting by Bluetooth or receiver. ProtoArc's EKM02 offers the wave idea for less, and the EKM01 Plus is its plainer sibling. SABLUTE adds a quiet set and a rechargeable set, and an unbranded 2.4G combo is the cheapest trial.
intro: A wireless combo should free a desk, yet many cost you two USB ports. Some sets pair keyboard and mouse through one tiny receiver; others ship a dongle for each, and on a thin laptop with two ports that is the difference between a clean setup and a hub purchase. Listings in this price range often leave it vague, so the single dongle question is the first thing to settle.

The second is how much ergonomics you actually get. A wave keyboard and a vertical mouse change posture; a generic curved set mostly changes appearance. We ranked six wireless ergonomic sets on paper, comparing keyboard shape, mouse design, power type, noise claims and price bucket. The Logitech pair is counted once, although it sells in two colors.

products.name: Logitech Wave Keys Keyboard and Lift Mouse Ergonomic Combo - Graphite
products.verdict: A matched wave keyboard and vertical mouse that connect either way.
products.description:
Logitech's graphite set earns first place by treating both hands. The Wave Keys keyboard curves its key rows to follow the arc of your fingers, and the Lift mouse is vertical, turning the hand to a handshake position so the forearm stops twisting. Both connect over Bluetooth or a receiver, and the design is matched, so the desk looks coherent. It sells in the $50 to $100 bucket.

It tops the ProtoArc sets because the vertical mouse is a genuine posture change, not a styling choice. The cost is a higher price than the budget sets below.

Buy it if you want an ergonomic upgrade for keyboard and mouse together. The caveat is practical: confirm on the current listing whether it ships with one dongle or two, and expect a few days of adjustment on the vertical mouse.
products.idealFor: A full ergonomic upgrade from one brand.

products.name: ProtoArc EKM02 Wave Keys Ergonomic Wireless Keyboard and Mouse, Black
products.verdict: A wave-style wireless combo at a lower price point.
products.description:
The ProtoArc EKM02 is how you get the wave layout without paying Logitech prices. It is a wireless ergonomic keyboard and mouse combo with wave-style keys, sold at the lower end of the $50 to $100 bucket. A wave keyboard sits between a flat slab and a full split, which makes it easy to learn.

It ranks second because it matches the wave concept of the Logitech set for less money. The trade is the mouse: it is a more conventional ergonomic shape rather than a Lift-style vertical design, so it relieves less forearm twist.

Choose it if you want the wave keyboard on a tighter budget and do not need a vertical mouse. The caveat is thinner brand detail, and the listing asks you to verify whether the combo uses a single receiver or two before you order.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who want a wave layout.

products.name: ProtoArc EKM01 Plus Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard Mouse Combo, Gray Black
products.verdict: A budget friendly wireless ergonomic set from a focused brand.
products.description:
ProtoArc's EKM01 Plus is the plainer cousin. It is a wireless ergonomic keyboard and mouse set in the $50 to $100 bucket, described as budget friendly, and it comes from a brand that focuses on ergonomic gear. Keyboard and mouse are sold together, so setup is a single purchase.

It ranks third behind the EKM02 because its listing gives fewer design details, though it costs about the same. For most buyers the two are close, and the extra specifics on the EKM02 tip the decision. Neither offers a vertical mouse.

Pick it for a straightforward ergonomic pair if the price is right. The caveat is how little the listing says about the shape of the keyboard and mouse, so check photos closely, and verify the dongle count, since the arrangement decides how many USB ports it uses.
products.idealFor: A simple ergonomic upgrade on a budget.

products.name: SABLUTE MA41 Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, 30dB Quiet Ergonomic
products.verdict: A budget combo that states a 30dB quiet rating.
products.description:
SABLUTE's MA41 is the quiet combo. It pairs a wireless keyboard and mouse in the $25 to $50 bucket and states a 30dB quiet rating on the listing. That matters in shared rooms and on calls, where a mouse click and keyboard clatter are heard by everyone.

It ranks fourth because the 30dB figure comes from the maker, not an independent source, so it is a claim rather than data. It is cheaper than the sets above it, though, and the ergonomic design is a mild one, closer to a curved keyboard than a wave.

Choose it for noise-sensitive spaces on a limited budget. The caveat is that you should not expect Logitech-level refinement. Verify whether the pair shares one receiver or needs two, and treat the noise number as marketing until you hear the keys yourself.

products.name: SABLUTE Ergonomic Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, Rechargeable
products.verdict: A rechargeable ergonomic pair that skips disposable batteries.
products.description:
This second SABLUTE set drops disposable batteries. It is a rechargeable ergonomic keyboard and mouse combo with a matched design, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Rechargeable power means no AA runs, and the wireless link keeps the desk clear.

It ranks fifth because it costs more than the MA41 without a stated noise rating, so you are paying for the battery convenience and not for quiet. Against the Logitech pair, it has a matched design but offers no vertical mouse or Bluetooth.

Pick it if you dislike buying cells and want a tidy, battery-free desk. The caveat is price against the budget sets. If cost is the only goal, the MA41 or the unbranded combo wins, and you should still confirm on the listing how the devices connect.
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants a battery free desk.

products.name: Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, 2.4G Ergonomic Wave Keys, Black
products.verdict: The cheapest wave-style 2.4G combo in this ranking.
products.description:
The last entry is an unbranded 2.4G wave-shaped combo, black, and the cheapest set in this ranking at $25 to $50. It includes a wave keyboard and a matching mouse over 2.4G wireless, which is a stable, widely used link.

It comes last because the brand gives you little to go on: no name behind it means less about warranty, support and long-term quality. Every other set here has a clearer identity, even the ProtoArc sets that cost nearly twice as much.

Buy it as a cheap trial of a wave layout before committing to a better set. The caveat is trust. Verify whether it uses a single dongle or two, and keep expectations modest on key feel, because the price leaves little room for refinement.
products.idealFor: A cheap trial of an ergonomic layout.

whatMatters.detail: Some combos share one receiver for keyboard and mouse, others ship two, and two receivers take two USB ports, which matters on a slim laptop. The listings here tell you to verify, so do. Read the bullets and images carefully, because one dongle versus two changes your port budget, and look at the box contents photo or the answers section before ordering.

A vertical mouse turns your hand to a handshake position, easing the forearm twist that a flat mouse forces. It takes a few days to learn and can feel odd at first, with slower pointing. Look for the word vertical in the product name, as in the Logitech Lift, and do not assume a curved mouse is vertical, since many ergonomic mice only tilt slightly.

A wave keyboard curves the key rows to match the arc of your hand. It is gentler than a split design, so the adjustment is shorter, and it suits most typists. Check the listing images for the curve and the shape of the key rows, since some ergonomic labels mean only a slight angle and do little for the wrist.

Rechargeable sets skip disposable cells, which saves money and waste, but you must remember to charge them. Look for the word rechargeable in the title and check the charging port type. Battery-powered sets need spares on hand, so factor in the recurring cost when comparing price buckets over a year.

A decibel figure suggests how loud the keys and clicks are. A maker-stated number like 30dB is a claim that the listing does not verify, and key weight and desk surface change real noise. Compare it with the switch type, and prefer sets that name their key mechanism and give a measurement method.

faq.q: Do both devices share one dongle?
faq.a: It varies by set, and the listings tell you to verify. Check before ordering, especially for the Logitech set or any combo like the ProtoArc EKM02, when USB ports are scarce on your laptop.

faq.q: Will a vertical mouse feel odd?
faq.a: For a few days, yes. A vertical mouse like the Logitech Lift feels odd until the hand adapts. Give it a week before judging, and keep the old mouse nearby for the first days in case of deadlines.

faq.q: Is the Logitech combo worth it over the ProtoArc EKM02?
faq.a: If you want a vertical mouse and Bluetooth, yes. If you only want a wave layout, the ProtoArc EKM02 costs less and still gives you a curved keyboard and a wireless pair.

faq.q: How do I connect a wireless combo?
faq.a: Plug in the receiver or pair over Bluetooth, then switch both devices on. For the Logitech set you can use either method, while the ProtoArc and unbranded 2.4G sets rely on a receiver, so mind your free USB ports.

faq.q: How do I keep it running?
faq.a: Charge rechargeable sets such as the second SABLUTE regularly, and keep the receiver close to the devices, ideally on a short extension port. Avoid placing it behind a metal case or a monitor base, which can weaken the signal.

It is stated by the manufacturer, so treat it as a claim, not an independent measurement. The SABLUTE MA41 lists 30dB, but key feel, typing force and the desk surface change how loud it sounds in practice.

finalTake: Buy the Logitech Wave Keys and Lift combo if you want a real posture change from one maker, or the ProtoArc EKM02 to get a wave layout for less. Pick the SABLUTE sets for quiet or rechargeable use, and the unbranded 2.4G combo only as a cheap experiment. Check the dongle count on any of them before ordering.
